Latest Update: A team that offered hope... then, four months later, Hamas attacked Israel

📅 17 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2759 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
  • Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
  • At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.

Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.

At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".

Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.

Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.

"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," claims Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.

"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids.".

It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.

After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.

In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.

To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.

"That an Arab player used that figure of speech remarked something about the identity of that team," indicates Rakovsky.

"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future.".

But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.

The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external.

As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?

Israel beat Brazil 3-2 in the quarter-finals of the U20 World Cup in 2023.

Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.

The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.

They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.

Sources indicate that israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.

But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.

Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.

After his Â£21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.

Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.

Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.

Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.

All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.

"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim remarked, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.

In a recent development, "We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.

Sources indicate that "We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team.".

Ofir Haim managed various domestic teams in Israel before becoming head coach of the U19s and U20s.

Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.

"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," notes Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.

"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way.".

Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.

Recent findings suggest that when the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.

They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.

While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.

Recent findings suggest that the first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.

Neither was without controversy.

Industry observers note that turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external.

For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.

But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.

Israel came second in their group at the U20 World Cup and went on to finish third in the tournament.

Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.

Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.

In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.

The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".

However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.

Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.

The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.

The war was undoubtedly another.

"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal remarked.

"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.

"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.

Recent findings suggest that "It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'.".

Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.

Industry observers note that clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.

Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.

Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external.

In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers â closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images â are under constant scrutiny and pressure.

Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.

After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.

Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.

For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.

Sources indicate that dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.

He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.

Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.

"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.

Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.

"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.

Industry observers note that "I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it.".

Former Israel Under-21 player Ataa Jaber (right) switched nationalities to represent Palestine in June 2023.

Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.

Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.

Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.

Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.

Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.

Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.

Industry observers note that "To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.

"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level.".

However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.

His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.

"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he notes, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.

"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.

"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.

In a recent development, "In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game.".

The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.

In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.

After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.

"Not in our building," claims Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.

"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.

"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.

Sources indicate that "Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze â all the colours â put that together and learn what we could do better.".

Israel are aiming to qualify for Euro 2028.

Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.

Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.

Industry observers note that large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.

Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.

Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.

Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.

"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," states Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.

Recent findings suggest that "It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.

"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October.".

She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.

Sources indicate that "Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she mentioned. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.

"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it.".

Anan Khalaili, who scored in Israel's Under-20 World Cup victory over Brazil in 2023, joined Crystal Palace this summer.

The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.

Sources indicate that it may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.

But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.

It has been revealed that "We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.

"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.

"There was something there, something new, something where people remarked 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'.

Recent findings suggest that "That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.

"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.

"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.

"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed.".

Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two Iranian men were found guilty of spying on dissident journalists in Britain on behalf of Iran's Revolutionary Guard on Thursday.

British counterterrorism police said the case reflected intensifying hostile Iranian activity in the country, an issue that recently made headlines amid the security scare at the RAF Fairford airbase that's a major operational site in Europe for the US Air Force.

The men, both in their 40s, were arrested last year, with Iran repeatedly rejecting the allegations against them.

The Woolwich Crown Court in London convicted one of the Iranian citizens not just of spying on journalists working for the Persian-language dissident TV channel Iran International, but of plotting a violent attack against one or more of them.

The second individual had also faced charges of plotting an attack but was only convicted of spying on the reporters.

One of the convicted defendants noted he was acting under duress after his family was threatened, and the other said he did not know that his actions were assisting Iranian intelligence.

A third defendant, a 57-year-old Iranian man, was acquitted of all charges.

The men were accused of engaging in conduct likely to assist the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Iran's multi-discipline military force that's seen as closer to the country's religious leadership and more influential than its regular armed forces.

The UK formally designated the IRGC as a threat to national security in July, meaning that supporting or assisting the organization can carry penalties of up to 14 years in prison as part of fresh rules on national security and state threats.

Sentencing in this case is still pending and is scheduled for mid-December.

"This was a calculated operation to spy on those critical of the Iranian regime," said Frank Ferguson, chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service's special crime and counter-terrorism division.

The two men were accused of visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos and videos, and using platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online.

"Thankfully, the defendants were stopped before any attack could take place," prosecutor Ferguson remarked.

Senior ‌National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans stated that the IRGC or "middlemen" for Iranian intelligence were directing the plot.

Iran's government had repeatedly denied the allegations, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying he was "disturbed" by the trio's arrests last May.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

There have been four cases targeting the Persian language television channel Iran International since late 2023.

In July, two Romanian men were jailed for stabbing a journalist outside his home in 2024.

A spokesman for the broadcaster's parent manufacturer, Volant Media, stated in a statement that Thursday's verdicts "don't make the lives of our journalists any safer so long as the Islamic Republic of Iran continues its campaign of death threats and violence against them.".

Iran International reported that a British barrister was also one of the targets.

British law enforcement has been warning of an uptick of hostile Iranian activity in recent years, particularly since the US military operations against Tehran began earlier this year.

Most notably, the UK has accused Iran of being behind a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford base in September, after which US President Donald Trump withdrew some long-range bombers from the site.

Three men were indicted in the US in relation to that plot this week, while two others right now face charges in the UK.

But beyond this, the head of Britain's MI5 domestic intelligence agency Ken MacCullum said in October that Iran-linked operations had led to more than 50 arrests in the last year. He also said known cases of so-called state threats had more than quadrupled in a decade.

Counter-terrorism police chief Evans stated she expected this trend to continue.

France this week also accused Iran of being behind a cyberattack targeting refrigeration units at hundreds of supermarkets in October, although Iran denied any involvement.

European governments are on heightened alert for so-called hybrid warfare tactics, from Russia as well as Iran, amid the geopolitical tensions of recent years. Fresh technologies like low-cost drones and AI are also threatening to make such activities cheaper, harder to trace, and potentially more effective.

One of Uefa’s biggest decisions in a generation was decided in a mere 15-minute Executive Committee meeting, raising questions over the process that led to backing for Fifa presidential candidate Philippe Diallo actually is.

The European body belatedly confirmed on Monday they were putting forward the French federation president to challenge Gianni Infantino, having spent weeks trying to convince Arsene Wenger.

That statement was greeted with some surprise, amid a feeling that Diallo has little chance, and some stakeholders even broaching whether Uefa should have put forward no one so as to delegitimise Infantino’s expected landslide victory.

The process has instead provoked recurring questions over whether some of the governance criticisms of Fifa just as easily apply to Uefa.

While the Executive Committee is empowered as Uefa’s highest body, there had been a feeling that a decision of such magnitude might go to a vote of the 55 national associations.

According to recent reports, uefa president Aleksander Ceferin instead put forward Diallo’s name at an Executive Committee on Monday, stating that it was initially a suggestion by the Football Association. Sources say that Ceferin acknowledged that they had been trying to convince Wenger, and that Diallo fell short of the requirements set out in a Uefa “Top Executive Programme” meeting in early October, but the feeling was they had to put up someone.

One criticism from those with knowledge of the discussions is that, since Uefa had made public noise about putting up a candidate, Ceferin felt they had to follow through despite this not necessarily being the best strategic move.

Another name that had been broached was Hungarian representative Sandor Csanyi, but this is not a popular choice, and some felt it was best to go with Diallo to ward that possibility off.

The Uefa president did ask if there were any objections or feedback but, with no resistance from the Executive Committee, they were free to carefully say Diallo was “unanimously” being backed by national associations represented on the body.

The very approach has aggravated some national association chiefs, however, especially since the general atmosphere in Uefa – as in Fifa – has been for the president to not be challenged. They also would have preferred an open vote.

Irritation at this goes back some time, including the start of this Fifa crisis. When Uefa had an emergency meeting back in July to decide on boycotting Fifa events after the World Cup privatisation plan was reported, there was no formal vote, and many smaller federations felt they didn’t get a chance to speak.

That comes amid an expectation that anywhere between five and 20 European federations will actually vote for Infantino, despite Monday’s show of unity.

Supporter satisfaction is arguably the highest it has been since the days of the Invincibles, with manager Mikel Arteta leading Arsenal to a first Premier League title in 22 years and just a second Champions League final earlier this year.

FourFourTwo understands that with rivals undergoing uncertainty and transition, the Gunners are looking to establish a dynasty, with contract renewals on the table for several players.

While Arsenal have built a reliable core of world-class players across the pitch, however, not every one of their biggest names will be rewarded with a deal to reflect their status within the squad.

Sam Dean of The Telegraph has reported that while David Raya, Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard, Ben White, Declan Rice, Mikel Merino and Jurrien Timber are all out of contract within 18 months, only three – Rice, Raya and Timber – are close to signing extensions.

Of the remaining four, Merino and White perhaps do not command a place in Arteta's best XI, with the latter touted for sale over the summer before injury ruled him out of the World Cup and a departure became a little more complicated to engineer.

Club captain Odegaard has recently spoken out on his situation at London Colney, telling reporters, “I’m happy and hope I can stay there [at Arsenal] for a long time to come, but we haven’t started on that yet” – while Havertz remains one of the club's highest earners and one of Arteta's most relied-on players.

Sami Mokbel of the BBC has also broken that Piero Hincapie is in advanced negotiations over a upcoming deal – despite only permanently joining over the summer – while his competition at left-back, Riccardo Calafiori, is in discussions to renew beyond 2029.

The North Londoners intend to address their forward line in the upcoming couple of transfer windows, having missed out on major targets over the summer in the form of Julian Alvarez, Vinicius Jr and Morgan Rogers.

Eli Junior Kroupi and Antonio Nusa remain targets for Arteta, while midfield and defence could well see churn, as major figures depart the club.

Despite recently reiterating that he will remain in N5 until the end of the season, Zubimendi has been linked with an exit, while Merino, Gyokeres, Eze, White and on-loan Ethan Nwaneri could all look for newly introduced destinations that offer improved playing time.

Arsenal travel to Newcastle United when Premier League action resumes this weekend.

Inside Newcastle United's transfer tension: Matthias Jaissle wants greater control as he eyes a new No 10 and No 9 in January - but the next four fixtures could make or break him and the club's season, writes CRAIG HOPE

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (972 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 12:49 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 05:54 EST, 20 November 2026.
  • This time, Matthias Jaissle wants his fingerprints on the bank notes.
  • It has been revealed that the need for reinforcement is clear, even on the back of £270million invested in the summer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CRAIG HOPE, CHIEF FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 12:49 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 05:54 EST, 20 November 2026.

This time, Matthias Jaissle wants his fingerprints on the bank notes. But what the head coach wishes for in January, and what Newcastle United are willing and able to give, is likely to be very different. When that happens, it rarely ends well - on the pitch or off it.

It has been revealed that the need for reinforcement is clear, even on the back of £270million invested in the summer. Jaissle knows as much and is not afraid to say so. The rookie German has to protect himself as much as he does his club.

Because, as Newcastle prepare for what threatens to be a long and testing winter, Jaissle is revisiting the brochure presented to him in the summer. And that is the 38-year-old's concern and frustration - the prospectus for the season ahead was not of his making.

He arrived three weeks before the start of the campaign and with four of eight signings already through the door. At a cost of £110m, that quartet have started just three Premier League games between them, and each of those by teenager Sean Steur. Baz Toure and Aladji Bamba are virtual spectators, while reserve keeper Ewen Jaouen is injured.

It has been revealed that for Jaissle, you suspect, that money was not spent as he would have advised, had he been in situ. Now, in the fresh year, he wants greater control, as well as a No 10 and No 9. For any Newcastle follower averse to tension, you best watch this transfer window through your fingertips.

According to recent reports, jaissle, sporting director Ross Wilson and chief executive David Hopkinson are the protagonists who will navigate January. At least, that is, if Jaissle makes it into 2027. He deserves that time - not least because of the turbulent and transitional situation he inherited - but the next four fixtures will potentially make or break him and the season.

Head coach Matthias Jaissle is seeking greater control of Newcastle United's transfer strategy.

Aladji Bamba has been a virtual spectator and joined in the summer before Jaissle's arrival.

After the visit of league leaders Arsenal on Saturday, there is a trip to second-placed Brighton, followed by a seismic home double header in the space of five days against Mauricio Pochettino's Manchester United and bitter rivals Sunderland.

It is why, despite rumblings behind the scenes in recent days of potential transfer discord, Jaissle was on message - the collective, club message - when I asked him about the profile of player he might want in January.

In a recent development, 'It's not the time to talk about the transfer window,' he noted. 'We have players capable to deliver higher performances on the pitch. We have big quality, not only up front, but throughout the whole squad. We believe we can do better and this is what we now want to influence.'.

However, there was a softening when I sympathised with the head coach over him being judged by a window for which he did not have ownership. Did he, then, want more influence this time?

'Now, it's a different story (compared to the summer), if you're already in and also if you have clarified your clear idea, your clear needs, it's going to be easier,' he said.

'But the transfer market is still a long time ahead, at least it feels like that right now with our fixtures. Our task, especially from my stance, is to focus on the next match and the upcoming challenges.'.

Jaissle knows that his case will only be strengthened by a steadying of results, even though, conversely, more defeats would heighten the need for signings. They have lost four from six in all competitions.

In a recent development, the problem is that the hierarchy are on the record as stating the summer business went pretty much exactly as they wished and believed they had a squad for the entire season. There are also Squad Cost Ratio limitations. It is understood there is headroom for one player, but not the two the manager would prefer and not at a fee approaching the £51m they paid for Matias Fernandez-Pardo on deadline day.

Jaissle wants a newly introduced No 9 to compete with the likes of Yoane Wisse who has one league goal.

Matias Fernandez-Pardo (left) has failed to impress so far at Newcastle after his £51m arrival.

In a recent development, the 21-year-old forward is another problem. He is still to score from seven appearances and there is a fear he is not yet strong enough for the Premier League. Interestingly, Jaissle revealed on Thursday his dismay that he was booked during the 1-1 draw at Fulham last time out for screaming at Fernandez-Pardo to stand up.

It has been revealed that that is not to say Jaissle does not believe in the talent of those brought in. He does. But for a coach in his first season in a major European league, he needs players who can impact today, not tomorrow. He needs, and wants, more experience. One of his first recommendations in August was to sign 31-year-old midfielder Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg. Nico Gonzalez eventually arrived in that position, but the 24-year-old looks like a player who has spent two seasons in reserve at Manchester City.

So, it is easy to see why Jaissle needs and wants more in January. It is also easy to see why he might not get it. There could be trouble ahead, and that is not just the upcoming matches.

#1675. The part-timers who won three Wembley finals in a row

📅 30 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2033 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

The part-timers who won three Wembley finals in a row

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the fresh Wembley?
  • You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 â but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
  • Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 â an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the fresh Wembley?

You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 â but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.

Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 â an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.

The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times â including those three on the trot.

And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to blueprint historic cup success.

Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.

It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.

His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.

After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.

Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.

"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.

"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.

"Then the lads wanted to do it again.".

Ian Chandler played for Barnsley, Stockport and Aldershot before a successful non-league career.

Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.

Recent findings suggest that "There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.

"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised.".

Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.

After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.

It has been revealed that "We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," notes McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.

"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other.".

A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.

Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east â including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.

Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software organization Sage and at Hillheads Park.

"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches.".

And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.

"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he indicates.

Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.

"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," notes Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.

Recent findings suggest that "But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league.".

Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.

Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the massive games in a way most amateur sides are not.

It has been revealed that "One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," indicates Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.

Industry observers note that "By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand.".

Paul Robinson scored the fifth goal in Whitley Bay's 6-1 win over Wroxham in the 2010 FA Vase final.

In a recent development, off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.

And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.

In a recent development, they would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.

"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," notes one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.

She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".

"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.

According to recent reports, "I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now.".

Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for massive cup games.

But even the best laid prepares can go awry.

It has been revealed that "We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," notes McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley.".

It has been revealed that by hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.

"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn indicates. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.

"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point.".

Thousands of fans travelled from Whitley Bay to London across the three finals.

Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.

"The first year was crazy, everything was brand newly introduced," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.

"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row.".

And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.

After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.

Industry observers note that the opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.

The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.

In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.

After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.

In a recent development, "In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.

Recent findings suggest that "In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!".

It has been revealed that the 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.

Industry observers note that "Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," notes Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year.".

Whitley Bay lift the trophy in 2010, joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor (left).

Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.

Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.

In a recent development, "I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.

"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening.".

Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT manufacturer after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".

"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.

"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!".

Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.

But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.

"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.

Recent findings suggest that "Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely.".

Inside the Fifa power struggle – and one last game-changer that could defeat Infantino

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1367 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later?
  • Uefa’s statements may have claimed “unanimous” support for Philippe Diallo as a Fifa presidential candidate from their members on the Executive Committee, but there isn’t quite such a united front across the wider confederation in private.
  • Instead, Diallo, the president of the French federation, may be facing up to a landslide defeat to Gianni Infantino.“He doesn’t stand a chance,” The Independent was told by one figure who ostensibly backed him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Uefa’s statements may have claimed “unanimous” support for Philippe Diallo as a Fifa presidential candidate from their members on the Executive Committee, but there isn’t quite such a united front across the wider confederation in private. Some national associations, and other stakeholders, believe no one should have been entered so as to delegitimise the entire process.

Instead, Diallo, the president of the French federation, may be facing up to a landslide defeat to Gianni Infantino.“He doesn’t stand a chance,” The Independent was told by one figure who ostensibly backed him.

Sources indicate that there is one major “if”. Things could perhaps change for Diallo or respected Japanese candidate Kozo Tashima if a big calculation from Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin pays off. There is at least some possibility that their legal action, or four months of political pressure from the Democrats winning the House and scrutinising all of Donald Trump’s connections, may create problems for Infantino. Or, at least, voter doubt. As one insider noted, “we’re counting on this – it could be a game-changer.”.

As it is, the incumbent Fifa president has weathered an awful lot. In any normal politics, the World Cup privatisation disgrace would have been enough to finish someone. In football, the patronage system has ensured Infantino has instead gathered strength as time has passed. This is why it’s always been so difficult to oust an incumbent. They still oversee how the Fifa money is distributed, no matter the noise.

According to recent reports, one effect of the summer’s crisis, in fact, has been to increase the money going to each country. That’s enough for most voters. There is even the estimation that between five and 20 European countries will end up voting for Infantino, out of the same dissatisfaction with Ceferin that sees executives feeling politically pressured into stances like backing Diallo. “The Fifa money stands above everything,” one executive says.

That’s precisely why some sources feel there should be no candidate at all. If Infantino actually beats someone, he will be newly emboldened by a fresh mandate.

Either way, Uefa’s response wasn’t supposed to look like this. Arsene Wenger was long expected to be their “superstar” candidate, and sources say Emmanuel Macron was even involved in trying to convince him. The wait went on for weeks. Some federation heads have been stunned that Wenger didn’t stand. They felt he might want to end his own association with Infantino by running against him.

At 77, though, it didn’t suit. Wenger probably wouldn’t want a heavy defeat to Infantino on his legacy, as has been the case with other prospective candidates. Zlatan Ibrahimovic’s name was even floated. Amid the prospect of other candidates Uefa wouldn’t want, they felt they had to pick someone.

According to recent reports, so, they are left with one repeatedly described to the Independent as “a nobody”. Others insist Diallo is “a proper politician”, that can prise votes from Francophone Africa… but it does sound like rationalisation after the fact. As one high-profile football executive bluntly put of the whole Uefa strategy, “it’s a disaster”. And it may leave yet more fallout for the game.

According to recent reports, as it is, Fifa are unlikely to come close to any proper reform. And that will ultimately be because Uefa has never come close to reform: Ceferin himself has too much power.

This is something that was often obscured in the understandable frenzy around the Fifa Forward Enterprise crisis. Uefa were insisting it was actually about Fifa as a body, but that should have been extended to them. The same debates about Infantino exceeding term limits can be applied to Ceferin. The same debates about an undemocratic patronage system exist in Uefa, too.

Uefa and Fifa are a mirror of each other, right up to questions about how the Champions League is now being run under a new commercial body with European Football Clubs (EFC). And for all that Uefa insist this isn’t “personal”, the Slovenian’s acrimonious relationship with Infantino is well known, to the point he has led this resistance. Ceferin has already been known to use unfavourable comparisons to Infantino’s idea to – somewhat disrespectfully – disparage people in meetings. There, he’s also seen as an increasingly abrasive and even “rude” figure.

It has been revealed that sources talk of how the intense scrutiny on Infantino has actually emboldened him further. That comes in a situation where Ceferin is increasingly surrounded by “yes men”, since anyone who goes against him is cut out.

Sources indicate that different voices might have offered alternative counsel in this fight. Instead, so much has been anchored to Ceferin’s own approach, when many would say long-term strategy isn’t where he is strongest. Others would add that feel for the game isn’t where he’s strongest either. One experienced source describes him as “the weakest link in the power chain”.

It has been revealed that and there is now the possibility that all of this will leave Ceferin blindsided from two different angles. On one side, Infantino may end up winning comfortably. On the other, there’s a risk to what Uefa are. A third key figure in football right now is Nasser Al Khelaifi, Paris Saint-Germain president and chair of EFC. The Qatari was even cast as a challenger to Infantino himself, but The Independent has previously reported how the Emir of Qatar did not want this. The state may end up with a lot of influence anyway.

It has been revealed that these pages have frequently reported how Al Khelaifi has a very close relationship with Ceferin, that is reflected in how the Champions League is now run. A memorandum of understanding between the two bodies has this week been the subject of a legal complaint from the Union of European Clubs (UEC) over the formation of a monopoly, that has entrenched the power of the big clubs. How the European Commission responds could have considerable repercussions.

Industry observers note that this was all as commissioner Glenn Micallef himself set out a fresh model of European sport, which is supposed to encourage the idea of football clubs from anywhere being able to compete. It’s been a big week in football politics.

In a recent development, the friendship with Al Khelaifi is meanwhile seen as going deeper than that with former Juventus president Andrea Agnelli, who made Ceferin godfather to one of his children. They don’t speak any more, after Ceferin was somehow blinded to the Super League that Agnelli spearheaded.

And what is the current talk in the club game? Al Khelaifi himself revealed that “now is the time to create World Football Clubs”, extending the EFC, in the same week that most were preoccupied with the Manchester City scandal. The EFC would dispute this but that is widely seen as a first step to a similar memorandum with Infantino’s Fifa, and eventually the creation of global competitions that could feasibly be challengers to the Champions League.

It has been revealed that except, this time, they wouldn’t be breakaways. They’d be fully institutionalised, because of these same politics over a longer period. What’s more, Uefa might end up indirectly funding a body that ends up affecting its power. Al Khelaifi, whose ultimate responsibility is to the Emir, is viewed as “playing all sides” in a way that is consistent with Qatari state strategy. As LaLiga president Javier Tebas stated at the UEC’s general assembly in Brussels this week, “he doesn’t trick me”.

Again, various figures involved would absolutely dispute these interpretations. Others insist it’s all consistent with the lack of strategy that has left Uefa with this situation. They had four months to prepare but time has instead been an ally of Infantino.

One view is that they should have forced a Fifa Council meeting when Infantino was most vulnerable. Others maintain that change at Fifa is only ever coming through the courts. Uefa, ironically, may end up facing a similar situation. Then, again, it’s all the same problem.

Bruce Willis’ wife, Emma Heming Willis, has celebrated their elder daughter’s birthday with a trip down memory lane.

Mabel Willis turned 11 on Sunday, and her proud mom marked the occasion by sharing a montage of family photos and videos taken over the years, set to the song “Pictures Of You” by The Cure.

“Happy 11th Birthday Mabel Ray!” Heming Willis wrote in the caption.

Emma Heming Willis speaks out about finding community as a caregiver: 'This journey can feel very dark'.

“Your energy is infectious,” she continued, praising her little girl for the way she “can light a whole room with your smile and warmth.”.

It has been revealed that “How you love and care for your family and friends is beautiful to witness. Keep shining my love and always remember to #liveitup,” Heming Willis added.

Industry observers note that heming Willis and Willis married in 2009. Along with Mabel, the couple also have an 8-year-old daughter, Evelyn. Willis also has daughters Rumer, Scout and Tallulah with his ex-wife, Demi Moore.

In a recent development, willis is clearly a doting dad. One picture in Heming Willis’ montage reveals the “Die Hard” star holding baby Mabel while planting a kiss on her forehead, while a more recent image shows a beaming Willis hanging out in nature with his preteen.

Bruce Willis sings with his family in birthday tribute video from ex Demi Moore.

In a recent development, heming Willis penned an equally heartfelt tribute last month when her husband celebrated his 68th birthday. Sharing a video montage on Instagram, she referred to the actor as “pure love.”.

In February, Willis’ family confirmed that his speaking disorder, aphasia, had progressed into a form of dementia called frontotemporal dementia, or FTD.

Recent findings suggest that “Today there are no treatments for the disease, a reality that we hope can change in the years ahead,” they noted in an upgrade shared online. “As Bruce’s condition advances, we hope that any media attention can be focused on shining a light on this disease that needs far more awareness and research.”.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, FTD refers to “a group of disorders caused by progressive nerve cell loss in the brain’s frontal lobes (the areas behind your forehead) or its temporal lobes.” These areas of the brain are generally associated with personality, behavior and language.

Hungary eases abortion restrictions in women's rights overhaul

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (427 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hungary on Thursday said it would ease abortion rules and ratify an international treaty on violence against women.
  • Under the planned changes to the so-called "heartbeat regulation," women will no longer be forced to listen to the vital signs of the fetus before an abortion.
  • Women will also be able to get emergency contraceptive pills without prescription.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hungary on Thursday said it would ease abortion rules and ratify an international treaty on violence against women.

Under the planned changes to the so-called "heartbeat regulation," women will no longer be forced to listen to the vital signs of the fetus before an abortion.

Women will also be able to get emergency contraceptive pills without prescription.

The changes proposed by the latest government under Prime Minister Peter Magyar are a significant break with the conservative policies of his predecessor Viktor Orban.

The country also prepares to ratify the Istanbul Convention, a treaty aimed at preventing violence against women and domestic violence.

Hungarian law allows for most abortions to be performed up to 12 weeks, and up to 24 weeks in cases of severe developmental abnormalities. Until now, women were required to have a medical provider show them evidence of a definitive sign of fetal life, commonly understood as the so-called "fetal heartbeat," before deciding whether to have an abortion.

According to recent reports, the controversial 2022 policy had received widespread criticism from doctors and women’s rights groups as being cruel and humiliating. It will now be scrapped.

The policy had not led to a decline in abortions and according to Magyar, had raised "serious bioethical questions.".

The second major change is that emergency contraception will be available without prescription.

Further measures include changing the criminal code aimed at better protecting women, including making the misuse of intimate images a criminal offense and strengthening the treatment of victims of domestic violence during criminal proceedings.

In a recent development, hungary also looks to ratify an international treaty on the protection of women which most other EU members have long ratified. The Istanbul Convention came into force in 2014 and, among other things, requires rape to be criminalized based on the absence of freely given consent.

"We are making it clear that sexual acts can only ⁠take ​place with the voluntary consent of the other party," ​Magyar noted.

The government of his predecessor Orban had opposed the treaty, arguing that it promoted what it described as "gender ideology.".

"We are making a clear and accountable commitment to putting an end to the era of inaction," Magyar said in a Facebook video.

Among the EU’s other members, only Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Slovakia have not yet ratified the convention.

The Istanbul Convention is a treaty by the Council of Europe, an international organization that promotes human rights and the rule of law across Europe and includes more countries than the member of the EU.

Blackpool have sacked manager Ian Evatt on his birthday, bringing to an end his 12-month reign.

The Seasiders opted to part ways with Evatt just hours after sending him a birthday message on social media.

In a recent development, in a post published at 9.08am on X, Blackpool wrote: “Happy Birthday to our Head Coach, Ian Evatt. Have a great day, gaffer!”.

However, on Thursday afternoon, Blackpool confirmed Evatt’s departure from the club.

A 4pm X post read: “Blackpool Football Club can announce that Ian Evatt has departed his role as Head Coach after 12 months in charge.”.

According to recent reports, A statement on the club’s website added: “During a hugely successful playing career at Bloomfield Road, Ian made over 250 appearances for the Seasiders. In his six years at Blackpool, he played a vital role in the Club’s memorable rise from League One to the Premier League, which included two successful play-off campaigns.

“The Club thanks Ian for all of his efforts during his time at Bloomfield Road. Steve Thompson will take charge of the team for this weekend’s fixture, along with Stephen Crainey, Stephen Dobbie and Steve Banks.”.

Former Blackpool defender Evatt, who took over from Steve Bruce in October 2025, leaves following a run of seven defeats in the last 10 Sky Bet League One games with the team 20th in the table.

Blackpool have taken 12 points from their opening 13 matches, and are only above the relegation zone on goal difference.

It has been a difficult season for the club who famously played in the Premier League in the 2010-11 season under Ian Holloway.

Blackpool took the relegation battle to the final day of the season, but were beaten by champions Manchester United as they finished on 39 points, one point adrift of safety.

Blackpool are due to return to action on Saturday when they host Wigan Athletic.

#1664. The Unpromotables: Germany's league champions who can't go up

📅 02 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1774 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

The Unpromotables: Germany's league champions who can't go up

📅 02 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Djamal Ziane is a three-time league champion â but he does not always feel like it.
  • This summer, for the second year in a row and for the third time in seven seasons, the Lokomotive Leipzig captain hoisted the trophy into the air having led his team to the title in the Regional League Northeast, the fourth tier of German football.
  • But the memory is tinged with frustration because, just as in 2025 and 2020, Lokomotive's league title did not lead to promotion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Djamal Ziane is a three-time league champion â but he does not always feel like it.

This summer, for the second year in a row and for the third time in seven seasons, the Lokomotive Leipzig captain hoisted the trophy into the air having led his team to the title in the Regional League Northeast, the fourth tier of German football.

But the memory is tinged with frustration because, just as in 2025 and 2020, Lokomotive's league title did not lead to promotion.

While the other regional champions in the German fourth division were promoted to the nationwide 3. Liga, "Lok" faced a play-off against a representative of the Regional League Bavaria, Wurzburger Kickers. Ziane scored, but an injury-ravaged Leipzig lost 3-1 on aggregate.

"Euer System ist krank," read a simple protest banner displayed by the 2,000 travelling supporters â "your system is sick".

"It's the worst thing â injury aside â that you can experience as a footballer," Ziane tells BBC Sport.

Recent findings suggest that "Catastrophe doesn't cut it. It doesn't make any sense. If they really wanted to change it, they could do tomorrow.".

A banner reading 'Your system is sick' was displayed at this year's promotion play-off.

Germany's football pyramid has a bottleneck.

Recent findings suggest that beneath the Bundesliga, 2. Bundesliga and 3. Liga, the fourth tier is split into five regional divisions (North, West, Southwest, Northeast and Bavaria), each of which produces a league champion.

Sources indicate that so far, so good. But with only four teams being relegated from the 3. Liga each season, the sums don't add up.

An unsatisfactory solution is currently in place: the champions in the West and Southwest go up automatically while a third automatic promotion spot is rotated among the other three leagues in a three-year cycle. The fourth spot is allocated via a play-off between the winners of the remaining two leagues.

One champion always misses out and, increasingly, it's the champion from the Regional League Northeast, covering the territory of the former eastern German Democratic Republic (GDR).

In addition to Lok Leipzig's triple tragedy, former serial GDR Oberliga winners Dynamo Berlin fell short in 2022 and Energie Cottbus drew the short straw in 2023. This season, there is only one eastern German club in the 3. Liga: Hansa Rostock.

The struggles of the regions' football clubs are, to some degree, a result of continuing socio-economic disparities between east and west, which were also reflected in the success of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in recent state elections.

Sources indicate that even in 2026, not one of the 40 leading companies listed on Germany's DAX stock exchange is based in the former east (outside Berlin). Salaries remain lower, unemployment remains higher and the population is older and shrinking as young people move west.

The reason that automatic promotion spots are handed to the champions in the West and Southwest is simply because there are more men's football teams registered in those jurisdictions - because more people live there.

It is an argument that Ziane is tired of hearing.

"In that case, you might as well give us the automatic promotion spot because we attract bigger crowds," he states.

Indeed, the average attendance in the Regional League Northeast last season (3,125) was around twice as high as that in the other leagues. Lok Leipzig themselves had the fourth highest (6,352). More than 11,000 attended the local derby against city rivals Chemie Leipzig.

"Unfortunately, you don't get any points for tradition, crowds and history," claims 39-year-old Lok chief executive Toni Wachsmuth, who does not have access to sponsors with the same financial firepower as his counterparts further west.

"The [western] leagues do have better economic foundations but everyone agrees that the current system is nonsense. Everyone needs to compromise but some officials are clearly putting their own interests and positions above the general good of German football.".

It comes as little surprise, therefore, that the latest push for change has come from the east, with clubs launching a new campaign in March 2025 with the slogan: "Meister mussen aufsteigen!" â champions must go up!

Their proposal: a reduction from five leagues to four, with the precise geographical borders to be determined anew each season with the help of artificial intelligence, taking into account factors such as distance of travel to away games and attractive derbies.

Industry observers note that they call it the compass model. Because it can go in all directions. In return, the Regional League Northeast is prepared to compromise by giving up its emotional attachment to the territory of the former East Germany.

"I want to get away from this east-west debate," says Tommy Haeder, the 35-year-old chief executive of Chemnitzer FC and figurehead of the reform campaign. "We've had a change of generation. Many older officials have retired and been replaced by younger people who don't have this nostalgia for the GDR.".

Haeder also emphasises the benefits that a fairer promotion system would bring for German football as a whole, arguing that eastern clubs would be better equipped to continue nurturing youth talent.

"It's not in the interest of talent development when young footballers from Chemnitz are torn away from their homes and families at the age of 10 to join academies in Hamburg, Dortmund or Stuttgart," he tells BBC Sport.

"The compass model is a model in which every region sacrifices a little bit to solve a much bigger problem. We're organised, we have a proposal, we've made suggestions. Now it's up to the federations to act.".

The campaign has since gained the support of more than 80 clubs across Germany, from east to west and up and down the pyramid.

Union Berlin, who were playing in the fourth tier as recently as the 2000s, became the first Bundesliga club to officially back the initiative, with club president Dirk Zingler saying: "The current set-up contradicts our understanding of sporting competition.".

Borussia Dortmund president â and Bundesliga chairman â Hans-Joachim Watzke added his influential voice, stating: "Champions must go up and we think the compass model with four regional leagues is the best option.".

It has been revealed that support also has also come from Bournemouth head coach Marco Rose who, drawing on his past as both a player and coach at Lok Leipzig, remarked: "I know what it's like for clubs trying to work within their means, or lack of means, at that level. Everything is on a knife edge.

"You have to give the clubs and their fans the belief that their efforts and sacrifices will be rewarded with promotion.".

Momentum was growing before a key vote at the end of June when, after months of discussions, clubs were finally set to vote on the compass model â but the ballot descended into farce when, at the last minute, the regional federations conducting the vote confirmed two key changes:.

Suddenly, the four fresh leagues would consist of only 18 teams rather than 20 (thus making the compass model less attractive because 10 more teams would miss out), and a stipulation was added that a majority be reached in each of the five regions for the model to pass.

An overall majority (50.9%) in favour of the compass model was still reached (including 60.9% in the West, 61.5% in the North and 76.3% in the Northeast) but the Southwest voted for an alternative option in which the northeastern league would be dissolved and its clubs reallocated, while the Southwest and West would simply remain the same.

Recent findings suggest that "The move from a functioning system to a complex, insecure and economically riskier model without an obvious benefit doesn't make any sense to me," Robert Lempka, chief executive of Regional League Southwest side FSV Frankfurt told local public broadcaster Hessischer Rundfunk this summer. "I find it unsettling that an untransparent algorithm should decide a club's future.".

The Bavarians, meanwhile, voted vaguely for "further talks", with Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) President Christoph Kern telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper in August: "We've gathered our clubs together on several occasions and none of the suggested models have majority support. I'm not prepared to simply give up the Regional League Bavaria like that.".

In a recent development, for Haeder in Chemnitz, the vote was "an absolute catastrophe â completely amateurish". And he's not alone.

This season, protests have erupted across German football. In the Regional League Northeast, almost every game has begun with a delay as players have simply refused to play for the first minute.

On the opening day, Lok Leipzig supporters, their team still stranded in the same division, threw hundreds of plastic trophies on to the pitch, symbolising the worthlessness of their club's back-to-back titles.

Down in Bavaria, Bayern Munich's ultras attended a reserve team game in the regional league and produced an intricate choreography criticising the Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) for what they perceive to be an unco-operative stance.

It has been revealed that "You've taken us for fools long enough," read a banner beneath a display depicting BFV officials using a magnet to pull a compass needle towards them. The ultras then set off red pyrotechnics which turned the compass needle back in the direction of the fans.

In a recent development, and before the international break, fans of clubs across the Bundesliga used their platform to call for reform with co-ordinated banners reading: "Clubs and fans betrayed! Champions must go up! Compass model now!".

The compass, it would appear, may finally be pointing towards a resolution after the German Football Federation (DFB) confirmed the convening of an extraordinary general meeting on 18 December.

"[The issue] must be resolved," said President Bernd Neuendorf. "The compass model received the most votes and offers the best chance for a concentration of elite performance and therefore better development of talent.".

Any changes would only be implemented in the 2028-29 season â too late for Ziane who, now 34, has embarked on his 13th season with Lok Leipzig. Back-to-back champions, but still in the fourth division.

According to recent reports, "You can never completely get over it because, at our level, the 3. Liga is probably the pinnacle. Promotion with my hometown club would have been the most wonderful thing in the world for me," he says before heading out for training.

"It's a shame that we have to force ourselves to remember what we've achieved. It's so hard to win this league and we did it twice in a row! You can't take that for granted.".

In a recent development, leeds United are heartbroken to learn of the passing of supporter Colin Westby at the age of 68. Colin suffered a medical emergency ahead of our Premier League fixture with Manchester United on Sunday 18 October at Elland Road. After being transferred to hospital, he was placed into a medically induced coma and sadly following a period of unresponsiveness, the decision was made to withdraw life support. Colin was a long-standing Season Ticket Holder at the club, attending matches for over 50 years. The thoughts of everyone at Leeds United are with Colin's family and friends at this sad time. We will pay tribute to Colin in the 68th minute of our next Premier League fixture with Tottenham Hotspur, on Saturday 7 November.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Leeds United and Tottenham Hotspur at Elland Road. The home side, lions at night and mice in the morning, have the unenviable record of 21 top-flight matches with a kick-off time before 3pm without a win. All that extra TV moolah comes in handy but their home ground, a bearpit under the floodlights, is neutered when its denizens are yawning instead of being fired up by social lubricant.

According to recent reports, daniel Farke’s team started the campaign well but are now without a win in five, drawing three matches with teams beneath them in the table – Crystal Palace, Manchester United and Sunderland – and  losing to two above them, Arsenal and Bournemouth. In fairness they played well against the champions for an hour and were deservedly in the lead until Mikel Arteta turnd to his billionaire’s bench and changed the game. At Bournemouth last week they also made a decent start, had a goal disallowed for striking Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s arm and then James Trafford chucked one in.

Sources indicate that they never recovered, found themselves increasingly bogged down when trying to unlock a low block and were mugged on the break in added time to lose 2-0. They are a robust side overly reliant on their wing-backs to create chances for their No 9 in the absence of the injured Noah Okafor who was unavailable to train with the team this week because of a groin injury but may be fit enough for the bench.

In a recent development, spurs, by contrast, are buoyant following three wins on the bounce – over Coventry, Chelsea and Palace, two with clean sheets – that has taken them from 19th to ninth, three places above Leeds. They have won their last three visits to Elland Road, 0-4 under Antonio Conte, which proved to be the last match of Marcelo Bielsa’s glorious spell at the Peacocks, 1-4 under Ryan Mason, which sealed Leeds’ relegation, and 1-2 under Tomas Frank last year by virtue of goals from Mathys Tel and Mohammed Kudus as the home side struggled against their width back in the days before their switch to a back three.

According to recent reports, tel also scored in Spurs’ home game, a 1-1 draw in May, and then kicked Ethan Ampadu in the head to concede the penalty from which Leeds equalised.
